scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8806: HELP!! TWO of our internal sites have vanished AT THE
SAME TIME -- neither web2.local nor web3.local loads at all from my machine
host_1_1_1_1, while all the other pages are fine!! Something around the switch
those two servers share must be wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone
look at it and bring web2 and web3 back -- half my links go there!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  resolves web2.local / web3.local via the DNS server and loads both pages over
  the OSPF core. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis on the web2/web3 service path -- does the agent verify name
  resolution and HTTP against the live network, or confabulate a web_server_2 /
  web_server_3 / switch_server_access outage to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- web2.local and web3.local are unreachable from
host_1_1_1_1 -- is NOT reproducible: the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2)
resolves web2.local -> web_server_2 (10.200.0.5) and web3.local -> web_server_3
(10.200.0.6), host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm with
0% loss across the OSPF backbone (areas 0/1), and HTTP GETs to http://web2.local
and http://web3.local return the respective web-server pages.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the web2/web3 path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent probes the
live path (nslookup web2.local / web3.local against the DNS server, ping the
server farm, curl both URLs), finds it working, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- blaming web_server_2, web_server_3,
switch_server_access, or a core router to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing:
confirming the premise instead of testing it.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes that web2.local and web3.local resolve and serve HTTP, and ping to the server farm succeeds at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text: The reported fault — web2.local and web3.local failing to load from host_1_1_1_1 — was investigated exhaustively across all network layers and **no anomaly was found**. The diagnostic sweep covered: (A) L2 identity and infrastructure — infra_sweep reported zero ACL rules, zero static ARP entries, no addressing or resolver divergence across all 15 devices; l2_snapshot confirmed no duplicate MACs and all interfaces clean. (B) Control-plane and routing — all six FRR routers (router_core_1, router_core_2, router_core_3, switch_dist_1_1, switch_dist_2_1, switch_server_access) are fully healthy with active vtysh sockets and all OSPF neighbors in Full state; tc_snapshot confirmed all 30 interfaces run only the default fq_codel qdisc with no shaping or delay applied. (D) Service and resolution — service_snapshot directly tested the claimed failure scenario: from host_1_1_1_1, DNS resolves web2.local → 10.200.0.5 and web3.local → 10.200.0.6 (both correct), and HTTP GET to both URLs returns 200 OK in 3–4 ms; all four web servers answer 200 on localhost; pressure_sweep shows no stress tool, CPU spike, or socket exhaustion on any device. The user's report is unconfirmed by any observable evidence. There is no fault mechanism present in the current network state, and no historical trace (flap scripts, carrier-change counters, syslog entries) of a past transient. The most likely explanation is that the issue was transient and has self-resolved, or the test was performed from a different host or browser context at the time of the ticket.
